title: How thermohaline circulation drives global ocean currents
dek: Why density differences from temperature and salinity power the planet's heat conveyor belt.
sentences: Surface ocean currents are driven largely by atmospheric winds, but deeper water movements are governed by a massive global conveyor belt.
This worldwide deep-ocean circulation system is known as thermohaline circulation, driven by differences in water density.
Water density in the oceans is governed by two fundamental factors: temperature and salinity.
Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is significantly denser than freshwater.
In the North Atlantic, warm surface waters transport vast amounts of tropical heat toward the polar regions.
As this water approaches the Arctic, frigid polar air chills it, and freezing sea ice leaves remaining water saltier.
This cold, exceptionally dense water sinks miles below the surface toward the ocean floor in a process called deep-water formation.
The sinking water pushes deep currents southward across global ocean basins, gradually warming and welling back up centuries later.
This conveyor belt regulates global climate by redistributing tropical heat toward higher latitudes and storing immense amounts of carbon.
Freshwater runoff from melting glaciers can dilute salinity in polar seas, threatening to slow this critical global circulation system.
A significant slowdown would dramatically disrupt European weather patterns and trigger severe marine ecological shifts.

keyPoints.concept: Density driven by temperature and salinity
keyPoints.statement: Thermohaline circulation is propelled by density differences: colder and saltier water is denser and sinks.
keyPoints.addHint: Explain the drivers of thermohaline circulation: cold temperatures and high salt concentration make water denser, driving the conveyor belt.
keyPoints.example: Thermohaline circulation is driven by density variations, where colder and saltier water becomes denser and sinks toward the seabed.

keyPoints.statement: Polar cooling and sea-ice freezing create dense water that sinks and pushes deep currents across global ocean basins.
keyPoints.addHint: Describe deep-water formation: polar air and freezing sea ice make water cold and salty, causing it to sink and drive global deep currents.
keyPoints.example: In polar regions, chilling air and sea-ice formation make surface water cold and salty, causing it to sink and drive deep ocean currents worldwide.

keyPoints.statement: The conveyor redistributes heat and carbon, but melting glaciers dilute polar salinity and threaten to slow the circulation.
keyPoints.addHint: Discuss climate impacts: circulation moves heat toward poles, but melting glacier freshwater reduces salinity and could slow the conveyor.
keyPoints.example: The circulation transports tropical heat to high latitudes, but melting glacial runoff can dilute salt levels and slow the conveyor belt.

commonMisconceptions.statement: Deep ocean currents are propelled primarily by atmospheric winds
commonMisconceptions.why: Winds drive surface waves and currents; deep-ocean circulation is driven by density differences from temperature and salinity.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Atmospheric winds drive surface water, but deep thermohaline currents are powered by density differences in temperature and salinity.

commonMisconceptions.statement: Warm water is denser than cold water and sinks to the ocean floor
commonMisconceptions.why: Cold water is denser than warm water, causing polar waters to sink.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Cold water is denser than warm water, which is why cold polar waters sink to drive the conveyor belt.
any: warm water sinks to the bottom

samples.label: Clear explanation
samples.text: The article explains how thermohaline circulation powers the global ocean conveyor belt. While surface currents are wind-driven, deep-ocean circulation is powered by density differences caused by water temperature and salinity. Cold and salty water is the densest. In the North Atlantic, tropical waters flow north, cool under frigid polar winds, and gain salinity as sea ice forms. This dense water sinks to the ocean floor and pushes deep currents across global basins over centuries. This system regulates global climate, but melting glacial freshwater could dilute polar salinity and slow the conveyor.

samples.label: Contains a misconception
samples.text: Deep ocean currents are powered primarily by atmospheric winds blowing across the globe. Warm water is denser than cold water and sinks to the ocean floor near the equator, which pushes water towards the poles to create circular currents.
